items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Evidence given by a person who saw an event, such as a crime, about what happened and who was involved”?

items.stem: Assertion (A): Target-absent line-ups are important in research on eyewitnesses. Reason (R): In real cases the police may have the wrong suspect. Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Children always make more errors than adults in every type of line-up. Reason (R): Children may feel pressure to choose someone. Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A 6-year-old, Lucas, saw a man steal a bicycle in a park in Dhaka. The police plan to show Lucas a line-up. Suggest one other way the police could make the line-up more suitable for a child.
items.answer: Use an elimination line-up (first choose who looks most like the thief, then decide if that person is the thief) or include a “not there” option such as a silhouette card.
items.markingKey: 1 mark procedure; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: A 6-year-old, Lucas, saw a man steal a bicycle in a park in Seoul. The police plan to show Lucas a line-up. (a) Explain why Lucas might identify an innocent person even if Lucas’s memory is good. (b) Suggest one other way the police could make the line-up more suitable for a child.
items.answer: (a) Social pressure: Lucas may want to please the adult questioner and assume they are expected to choose someone. (b) Use an elimination line-up (first choose who looks most like the thief, then decide if that person is the thief) or include a “not there” option such as a silhouette card.

items.stem: A 6-year-old, Omar, saw a man steal a bicycle in a park in Cape Town. The police plan to show Omar a line-up. (a) Explain why the police should tell Omar that the thief may not be in the line-up. (b) Explain why Omar might identify an innocent person even if Omar’s memory is good.
items.answer: (a) Children may feel they must choose someone; an unbiased warning reduces pressure and false identifications. (b) Social pressure: Omar may want to please the adult questioner and assume they are expected to choose someone.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A procedure in which a witness is shown a suspect among several other people (foils) to see whether they can identify the culprit”.

items.stem: A student writes: “A foil in a line-up is the person the police suspect.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. A foil is a known-innocent person who resembles the description; the suspect is the person police think may be the culprit.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a target-present and a target-absent line-up.
items.answer: In a target-present line-up the culprit is included among foils, so the correct response is to identify them; in a target-absent line-up the culprit is not included, so the correct response is to reject the line-up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, contrasted [2]

items.stem: “Pozzulo et al.’s (2009) study of children’s and adults’ line-up identifications has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including the use of target-present and target-absent line-ups in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The findings can inform how police conduct line-ups with child witnesses, for example by warning that the culprit may not be present or using procedures that reduce pressure to choose. Strength (the use of target-present and target-absent line-ups): Including both types of line-up shows not only whether witnesses can recognise a target but also whether they wrongly choose someone when the target is absent, which matches real police situations. Weakness (ethics): Children cannot give fully informed consent, so parental consent was needed, and children may feel anxious about being “wrong”. Weakness (generalisability): The children were a narrow age range from one area, so the results may not apply to older children or to children from other cultures. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Describe the general procedure of Pozzulo et al.’s study.
items.answer: Children and adults were shown target stimuli and then asked to make identifications from line-ups that were either target-present or target-absent; their identification decisions (correct identifications, false identifications and correct rejections) were compared.
items.markingKey: 1 mark groups; 1 mark TP and TA line-ups; 1 mark decisions compared [3]

items.stem: Describe the main finding of Pozzulo et al.’s study about target-absent line-ups.
items.answer: Children made more false identifications (and fewer correct rejections) than adults when the target was absent, even though they were similar to adults when the target was present.
items.markingKey: 1 mark TA more errors; 1 mark comparison with TP [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Pozzulo et al.’s (2009) study of children’s and adults’ line-up identifications. Include at least one point about ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (the use of target-present and target-absent line-ups): Including both types of line-up shows not only whether witnesses can recognise a target but also whether they wrongly choose someone when the target is absent, which matches real police situations. Strength (usefulness): The findings can inform how police conduct line-ups with child witnesses, for example by warning that the culprit may not be present or using procedures that reduce pressure to choose. Weakness (ecological validity): Watching stimuli in a study is not as stressful or emotional as witnessing a real crime, so identification accuracy may differ in real life. Weakness (demand characteristics): Children may believe the adult researcher expects them to choose someone from the line-up, so their choices may reflect social pressure rather than memory. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: In Nairobi, 9 children aged 5–6 and 9 adults each completed 10 target-absent line-ups; the number of correct rejections (saying “not there”) was counted. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that adults will make more correct rejections than children aged 5–6? Use the data in your answer. (d) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) IV: the age group of the participant (child or adult) — a naturally occurring IV. DV: the number of target-absent line-ups (out of 10) correctly rejected. (b) Children should be reassured and debriefed so that they do not feel they failed. (c) Mean for adults = 6.9 and children = 5.0; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 6 and 8) and the sample is small (n = 9 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. items.stem: Plan a laboratory experiment to investigate whether warning witnesses that the culprit may not be present reduces false identifications. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, the type of data collected, ethical issues and how the dependent variable will be measured.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: warning or no warning; DV: number of false identifications in target-absent line-ups. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Bangkok, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Evaluate Pozzulo et al.’s (2009) study of children’s and adults’ line-up identifications in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about standardisation.
items.answer: Strength (the use of target-present and target-absent line-ups): Including both types of line-up shows not only whether witnesses can recognise a target but also whether they wrongly choose someone when the target is absent, which matches real police situations. Strength (standardisation): All participants saw the same stimuli and were tested with the same line-up procedure and instructions, so children’s and adults’ performance could be compared fairly. Weakness (demand characteristics): Children may believe the adult researcher expects them to choose someone from the line-up, so their choices may reflect social pressure rather than memory. Weakness (ecological validity): Watching stimuli in a study is not as stressful or emotional as witnessing a real crime, so identification accuracy may differ in real life. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Evaluate Pozzulo et al.’s (2009) study of children’s and adults’ line-up identifications, including a discussion of ethics.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The findings can inform how police conduct line-ups with child witnesses, for example by warning that the culprit may not be present or using procedures that reduce pressure to choose. Strength (standardisation): All participants saw the same stimuli and were tested with the same line-up procedure and instructions, so children’s and adults’ performance could be compared fairly. Weakness (demand characteristics): Children may believe the adult researcher expects them to choose someone from the line-up, so their choices may reflect social pressure rather than memory. Weakness (ethics): Children cannot give fully informed consent, so parental consent was needed, and children may feel anxious about being “wrong”. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
